extracted.intended_audience: corporate communicators (IR), financial analysts, accounting/finance researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting corporate press releases that are likely to be used by sell-side analysts to revise forecasts and thereby increase pickup/propagation. Emphasizes disclosure content and form that fit analysts' decision processes and incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysts' economic incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysts are not passive receivers; they have economic incentives that shape how they read press releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that analysts interpret disclosures through the lens of their compensation, career concerns, and the needs of their clients/firms. Disclosure should anticipate incentive-driven behaviors (e.g., emphasis on actionable inputs) rather than assume neutral processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit to analyst decision needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Forecast quality depends on the fit between disclosed information and analyst decision needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design releases to supply the specific inputs analysts need for updating models and forecasts (not just narrative or totals). A release that fits decision needs is more likely to produce actionable analyst revisions and broader media pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid strategic/selective disclosure asymmetries
rubrics_metrics.description: Selective disclosure (pre-Reg-FD) created strategic information asymmetries that distorted both releases and forecasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimize selective/private disclosures that produce uneven information across analysts; prefer public, structured releases that reduce strategic ambiguity and unequal access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-relevance principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases should answer the questions analysts will ask in their forecast revision: revenue trajectory, margin trend, segment mix, capex plans, working-capital changes, guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly address core forecasting questions in the body or data tables so analysts don't need to infer or call IR. Include concrete items: revenue trends, margin drivers, segment composition, capital expenditure plans, working capital dynamics, and any forward guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forecast-supportive (bottom-up) disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Releases should enable a bottom-up forecast (segment-level data) rather than only top-line totals — sophisticated analysts work bottom-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide segment-level metrics and decomposition so analysts can build or update firm-level models from constituent parts instead of relying solely on aggregate figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconciliation to consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: Releases should explicitly reference the consensus expectation (or guidance) and explain the variance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State how reported results compare to published consensus estimates or prior guidance and explain principal reasons for any beats/misses to reduce ambiguity about earnings drivers and surprises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drivers, not just results
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the drivers of the result (volume, price, mix, currency, one-time) rather than only reporting the bottom line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decompose performance into causal contributors (e.g., volume vs. price vs. mix vs. FX vs. one-time items) because drivers determine the direction and magnitude of analysts' forecast revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forward-looking specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Where guidance is given, give it in a form analysts can model (range, base assumption, sensitivity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague qualitative guidance; provide numeric ranges, explicit base-case assumptions (e.g., FX rates, commodity prices), and sensitivity analyses so analysts can incorporate information directly into models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segment data sufficient for industry comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide segment-level data in a form comparable to peer firms' disclosures, so analysts can do peer benchmarking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format segment disclosures and KPI definitions to align with industry conventions and peer reporting to facilitate benchmarking and cross-firm model adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure consistency over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-defining segments or KPIs without bridging tables degrades analyst trust and triggers downward consensus drift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When changing definitions, provide clear bridging/recategorization tables and historical restatements so analysts can maintain consistent time series; abrupt, unexplained redefinitions undermine comparability and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Q&A pre-emption
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate the questions the analyst would ask if they could call (and many can't reach IR) and answer them in the release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include likely analyst questions and answers in the narrative or an FAQ section—especially where direct access to IR is limited—to reduce follow-up calls and clarify ambiguous points proactively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality calibration
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclose at a granularity that matches the materiality of the item; over-disclose on what's material, do not bury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose disclosure granularity so that material items are clearly visible and supported with detail; avoid excessive aggregation that buries material drivers or conversely overloading with immaterial minutiae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentive disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Compensation tied to specific metrics should be flagged so analysts understand the management-incentive context of the disclosed metric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When metrics are used in executive pay or other incentive schemes, disclose that linkage so analysts can assess potential management incentives to emphasize or manage those metrics.
